meta.title: Who really said "Tact is the ability to tell someone to go to hell in such a way that they look forward to the trip"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Churchill. It began as an anonymous newspaper filler joke about diplomats in the St. Louis Star-Times in November 1937, was popularised by the travel writer Caskie Stinnett in 1960, and only acquired Churchill's name on quote-sharing sites from about 2008.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Tact is the ability to tell someone to go to hell'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous 1937 newspaper gag about diplomats. Churchill's name was attached decades after his death, by crowdsourced quote sites.

answer.label: Not Churchill — an anonymous 1937 newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest located instance, St. Louis Star-Times, November 1937
answer.sourceLine: There is no Churchill source, and the joke did not start out being about tact at all — it was about diplomats. The earliest located instance is an unsigned filler item in the St. Louis Star-Times of November 1937: a diplomat is someone who can tell you to go to hell in such a tactful way that you look forward to the trip. It spread anonymously through the 1940s, was credited to the humorist Viola Layne in 1949, popularised by the travel writer Caskie Stinnett in 1960, and reworded from ‘a diplomat’ to ‘tact’ in the 1960s. Churchill’s name shows up on quote-sharing sites around 2008 — forty-three years after he died.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: A diplomat is a person who can tell you to go to hell in such a tactful way that you'll look forward with pleasure to making the trip.
trail: The 1937 Star-Times instance is a filler item — the unsigned one-liners newspapers used to plug the bottom of a column. Filler is where anonymous jokes live, and it is the least likely place on earth to find an unattributed remark by a sitting British MP the chronology ↗.

It travels by reprint. The same phrasing turns up in the Altoona Tribune, and by 1945 the De Kalb Daily Chronicle is running a shortened version with ‘pleasantly’ instead of ‘tactfully.’ In 1949 the syndicated columnist Earl Wilson gives it a first named author — the humorist Viola Layne.

In 1960 the travel writer Caskie Stinnett used it in his book Out of the Red, which is the version most often reprinted afterwards. Stinnett is frequently called the author; he was, on the record, a late populariser of a gag already twenty-three years old.

The switch from ‘a diplomat is…’ to ‘tact is…’ happens in the 1960s — the sportswriter Joe Williams is among those who move the joke onto tact itself. The Churchill credit arrives last of all, appearing on Goodreads around 2008 with no source attached, and spreads from there.
source.excerptNote: The 1937 filler, as printed. Two things to notice: it is a definition of a diplomat, which is the whole joke — professional courtesy as weaponised politeness — and it is longer and looser than the version we quote now. Seventy years of retelling tightened it and, at the very end, gave it an author.

source.rightsNote: The 1937 newspaper filler is anonymous and long out of copyright, so the joke in its original form is free to reproduce. Caskie Stinnett’s 1960 book Out of the Red is a separate, later work with its own status — quote the saying, not his page. And because the line is not Churchill’s, the constraint that catches people quoting him properly does not apply here: his genuine writings stay in copyright via his estate until 2035, but this is not one of them. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British statesman, historian and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill is the patron saint of the elegant insult, and he earned it — the genuine Commons exchanges are savage and beautifully built. So a joke about telling a man to go to hell charmingly has nowhere else to go. But that reputation is exactly the trap: because he really did say things like this, people stop asking for a source. The International Churchill Society keeps a searchable database of some 2.5 million of his words and publishes a standing list of things he never said, and this joke was printed in an American newspaper as anonymous filler while he was out of office and out of favour.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a joke being promoted. It starts anonymous, acquires a series of increasingly respectable owners, and finally lands on the most famous wit available — each step making it harder to check.

items.why: No speech, letter, article or reported remark. The Churchill attribution appears on crowdsourced quote sites from around 2008, which is forty-three years after his death and seventy-one after the joke was first printed the chronology ↗.
The travel writer used it in Out of the Red in 1960 and is often credited as its originator. He was working with material already in general circulation for more than two decades.

The columnist Earl Wilson credited the humorist Viola Layne in 1949. That is the earliest name anyone attached — but it is a columnist’s credit, twelve years after the joke was already in print, so we hold it loosely.

For its first quarter-century this was a definition of a diplomat. The ‘tact is the ability…’ form is a 1960s rewrite. If you are searching archives for the original, searching for ‘tact’ will find you nothing before then.

misattribution.truthLine: Anonymous. It first appears as a filler item about diplomats in the St. Louis Star-Times in November 1937, and only became Churchill’s in the age of quote-sharing sites the fact-check ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It flatters a skill most people would like to claim. Everyone has had to deliver bad news to someone who outranks them, and the joke turns that grim little art into a compliment — the tactful person is not a coward, they are a craftsman.

It works because of the collision in the middle of the sentence. ‘Go to hell’ is the bluntest thing in English; ‘look forward to the trip’ is a travel brochure. Putting them in one clause is the whole gag, and it is why the line survived seventy years of anonymous reprinting before anyone thought to sign it.
context.detailsSummary: The joke's career, step by step
detailsBody: November 1937: unsigned filler in the St. Louis Star-Times defines a diplomat.
Late 1930s–1940s: reprinted in the Altoona Tribune and elsewhere; by 1945 a shortened ‘pleasantly’ variant is running.
1949: Earl Wilson credits the humorist Viola Layne — the first named claimant.
1960: Caskie Stinnett uses it in Out of the Red, and becomes the version everyone reprints.
1960s: the subject shifts from ‘a diplomat’ to ‘tact’.
c. 2008: Goodreads carries it as Churchill, unsourced, and the internet takes it from there.
context.pull: For its first twenty-three years it was not about tact. It was a definition of a diplomat.
